_comment: Every tunable setting in Vessel is declared here, not in UI code. The
container editor renders this file with one composable per param type, so
adding a knob is a data change. Defaults are correct for the canoe target
'help' is shown next to the control. It must be one plain sentence that a
user who does not know what a translator is can act on. If a setting
cannot be explained that way, it does not belong in this file at all.
Nothing here is hidden any more: there is no 'advanced' flag and no
disclosure in the editor. That means ORDER IS THE HIERARCHY. Groups are
named for what a setting affects rather than for the subsystem that
implements it, and they run from the ones a user opens the screen for
(Display) to the ones that are correct until something breaks
(Compatibility). Put a new param where a user would look for it, not next
to the code that reads it.
For params of type 'component', the default is a selector, not a package
id: '@latest' resolves to the newest installed package of componentType.
Package ids are build outputs (dxvk-2.7.1-canoe) and must never be
hardcoded here, or a version bump would silently break every default.

groups.title: Display
groups.help: Desktop size, frame rate, and what opens on it.

params.title: Resolution
params.help: Lower is much faster, and it is the biggest dial on this phone: a game at 1280 x 720 measured 20-26 fps and the same scene at 640 x 360 hit the 60 fps cap. Halving each side quarters the pixels. Pick a size or type any WxH.

params.title: Frame rate limit
params.help: Only rates this screen can show. Lower keeps the phone cool.

params.title: Upscaler
params.help: How the guest's picture is stretched to fill the screen when Resolution is below it. Snapdragon Game Super Resolution reconstructs edges; Bilinear just blurs. Neither runs at all when Resolution already matches the screen.

params.title: Edge direction
params.help: Reconstructs a diagonal along the direction of its edge instead of evenly around it, which is most of what a 2x upscale does; Qualcomm rates the extra cost as minimal but it is not free.

params.title: Edge sharpness
params.help: How hard a reconstructed edge is pushed. Qualcomm's default is 2.0 and the result is clamped to the neighbouring pixels either way, so this cannot ring beyond them.

params.title: Edge threshold
params.help: How different neighbouring pixels must be before they count as an edge worth reconstructing, in 255ths. Higher is softer and faster because fewer pixels take the expensive path; Qualcomm's default is 8.

params.title: Maximum pixel change
params.help: The most any single pixel may be moved by reconstruction, in 255ths, which is also the size of any shimmer it causes on edges that keep crossing the threshold as the camera moves; Qualcomm's default is 23.

params.title: Multiple
params.help: Shows frames the guest never drew, predicted by the GPU from the last two it did, through GL_QCOM_frame_extrapolation. Frame rate limit becomes what the screen shows: the game is capped at that divided by this multiple, so 120 fps at 2x renders 60 and presents 120 — a game left to render flat out has no GPU left over to predict with. EXPERIMENTAL: on this device the driver accepts the call and reports no error, but the predicted frames come back as colour speckle, so turning this on shows dots and flicker. Everything behaves normally with it Off.

groups.title: Hardware
groups.help: What the guest is told this phone has. Every layer is configured from these, so Wine, FEX, the two D3D translators and the driver all report the same machine.

params.title: Cores
params.help: How many of this phone's eight cores the guest is told about. Six by default, which leaves two for Android, the translator and shader compilation; going lower has been measured to stall a game's launch while the code cache is being built.

params.title: RAM
params.help: How much system memory the guest is told it has. Games size streaming and texture pools from this, and the phone runs Android and the translator in the same memory, so six is a deliberate under-report rather than the fifteen the device has. Type a size the list does not offer if you want one: a bare number is gigabytes, and MB works too, so 1536 MB is sayable.

params.title: VRAM
params.help: How much video memory the guest is told it has. This phone shares one pool between CPU and GPU, so left to itself a game is told it has all of system memory and sizes its texture budget for a machine that does not exist. Set on the driver, so every graphics layer reports it. A bare number is gigabytes; MB works too.

groups.title: Compatibility
groups.help: One escape hatch for a single misbehaving program.

params.title: Use Zink for OpenGL
params.help: Sends OpenGL through the bundled Mesa driver instead of Wine's. Off is correct for almost everything, including Direct3D games -- one of them loads the OpenGL stack without ever calling it, and died on this. Turn it on only for a game that actually uses OpenGL.

params.title: Extra DLL overrides
params.help: Wine's WINEDLLOVERRIDES. Leave empty unless following specific advice.

groups._fixedNote: Thread synchronisation is NOT a setting. It is fixed to esync, the only mode that works here, and the session launcher must set it unconditionally. ntsync needs a kernel driver Android does not ship on any branch and sepolicy would block anyway. fsync is worse than unavailable: Proton probes it with the futex_waitv syscall, which is absent from Android's seccomp allowlist, and the default action is SECCOMP_RET_TRAP — so the probe SIGSYS-kills the process instead of failing gracefully. Offering fsync in the UI would have shipped a crash. See README, Known limitations.
groups._note: The three FEX memory-ordering toggles (TSOEnabled, HalfBarrierTSOEnabled, VectorTSOEnabled) used to live here and are now fixed in SessionEnvironment.kt alongside WINEESYNC. They were removed for the same reason as the Settings, Components and GPU-drivers screens: every default was already the only correct one, and each was a trade a user would be making blind. Measured on this device (tools/tso/run.sh, and see docs/ARCHITECTURE.md 'Why memory ordering dominates on this chip'): strict ordering is required for correctness, the half-barrier path is a 21% win over disabling LRCPC2, and vector ordering is a severe cost that fixes nothing on hardware without FEAT_LRCPC3 codegen. Nothing a user could learn from the UI would change any of those. If a future device or FEX release changes the answer, the value changes in code -- it does not come back as a switch.
